---
title: How SymEval works
---

SymEval sits on top of two libraries that each do one job well, and does nothing
more than connect them. [SymPy](https://docs.sympy.org/) holds the formula as
symbols, so you can rearrange or simplify it before any numbers exist.
[Pint](https://pint.readthedocs.io/) holds the numbers as quantities, so a value
carries its unit through every operation. SymEval evaluates the SymPy formula
with Pint quantities and writes it out as LaTeX.

## The three parts

Every symbolic evaluation shows the same three parts, the way a calculation is
written out to be checked:

1. **Symbolic form.** The formula shown with symbols, untouched.
2. **Substituted form.** Each symbol replaced by the Pint quantity you supplied,
   so the units are visible while the structure of the symbolic form stays
   intact.
3. **Result.** The evaluated quantity, converted to the output unit you asked
   for.

$$\begin{align*}
\sigma &= \frac{F}{A} \\
&= \frac{\,-680\ \mathrm{kN}}{\,10580\ \mathrm{mm}^{2}} \\
\sigma &= -6.43\times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{Pa} = -64.27\ \mathrm{MPa}
\end{align*}$$

The value of showing every step, rather than only the answer, is that a reviewer
can follow the reasoning: the formula is stated, the inputs are visible with
their units, and the result is traceable back to both.

## Why symbols and quantities are kept separate

Keeping the formula symbolic until the last moment is what lets you do algebra
first. Starting from the ideal gas law as an equation, SymPy can solve for any
variable before a single number is filled in:

$$P V = n R T \quad\longrightarrow\quad P = \frac{R T n}{V}$$

SymEval leans on this directly. Give `sym_evalf` a `sympy.Eq` and it solves for
the single unknown (the free symbol not present in your substitutions), then
evaluates. You never write the rearranged form by hand, so it cannot drift from
the equation you started with.

Keeping the numbers as Pint quantities is what makes the units correct rather
than merely annotated. Because each input is a real quantity, the substituted
form shows genuine units, unit conversions happen inside the evaluation, and a
mismatch (adding a length to a pressure, say) is an error rather than a wrong
number that looks plausible.

## Chaining one evaluation into the next

A single symbolic evaluation is useful; **chaining** several is where engineering
checks live. `sym_evalf` returns a `SymbolicEvaluation` whose `.symbol` and
`.quantity` are a plain SymPy symbol and a plain Pint quantity. So the result of
one step drops straight into the `subs` of the next, and each intermediate value
renders its own steps. A multi-step check becomes a readable sequence of
symbolic evaluations rather than one opaque number. The
[tutorial](getting-started.qmd) works through a chained calculation, feeding the
axial resistance of a steel member into a demand-over-capacity ratio.

## No bundled registry

SymEval defines no unit registry of its own. It reads the registry from the Pint
quantities you pass in, so every result lands in the same registry your inputs
came from. This keeps SymEval out of the way in a codebase that already has its
own `UnitRegistry`, and it means there is never a second, conflicting notion of
what a millimeter is. When there is nothing to read a registry from, SymEval
falls back to Pint's application registry.

## Rendering without a runtime dependency

SymEval renders through `_repr_latex_`, the same hook Jupyter and marimo already
look for. There is no dependency on a marimo runtime and no cell magic, so the
same `SymbolicEvaluation` object displays in a marimo notebook, a Jupyter
notebook, or anywhere else that understands the LaTeX representation. In plain
Python the object still holds the computed quantity and the rendered LaTeX as
attributes.
